prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer stands on a flat ground plane (dark background, roughly 1.5–1.8 m below the head-mounted camera), with their bright upper torso at the bottom edge (0.1–0.3 m away), shorts and legs extending downward (0.5–1.5 m), and both arms reaching forward into the scene (0.3–0.8 m). A small tan-and-white dog is on the ground in front of the wearer at roughly 1.2–1.5 m distance in frames 1–3 and 5, turning from facing left in frames 1–3 to jumping up toward the wearer in frame 4 (closing to about 0.6–0.8 m directly in front of the wearer's hands) before dropping back to the upper-left ground in frame 5 facing right, while looking up toward the wearer and the handheld blue-and-green dumbbell toy in frames 1, 2, 4, and 5. The toy remains held within the wearer's grasp—transferred from the extended left hand in frames 1–3 to both raised hands in frame 4 (roughly 0.4–0.5 m from the camera) and to the raised right hand in frame 5—coming within immediate reach of the leaping dog's mouth in frame 4 while the wearer's arms partially occlude their own legs and the dog's lower body. Compared to RGB alone, the depth gradient clearly quantifies the vertical elevation of the wearer's raised arms in frame 4 and the dog's mid-air proximity relative to the ground plane. However, the depth map is unreliable around the handheld toy in frames 1–3 (where the blue toy disappears into the dark background depth) and in frame 4, where the leaping dog is rendered anomalously dark and indistinct despite being elevated and closer to the camera.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map outlines the spatial footprints of the camera wearer's body at the bottom of all five frames (spanning roughly 0.1–1.5 m from the camera) and the dog in front of them on the concrete floor (roughly 1.2–1.5 m away on the ground, closing to 0.6–0.8 m in frame 4), while leaving the paved ground and drainage grate unsegmented in black. Across the sequence, the masks track the wearer's left arm extending forward-left in frames 1–3, both arms lifting centrally in frame 4 in front of the torso, and the right arm raising to the upper right in frame 5, while the dog moves from the upper-center/left in frames 1–2 to directly above the wearer's hands in frame 4 and to the upper-left in frame 5. The masks clearly show the spatial adjacency and partial occlusion in frame 4 where the wearer's raised left arm overlaps the lower edge of the leaping dog's head and paws at arm's reach (about 0.4–0.6 m from the camera). While segmentation helps isolate the silhouette of the wearer and the dog from the grey pavement, it is highly unreliable in class labeling and instance consistency: it misclassifies the dog as a 'bird' in frames 1, 2, and 5 and as a 'person' in frame 4, and completely fails to detect the dog in frame 3 or the handheld toy in any frame. Furthermore, the wearer's single body is over-segmented into multiple separate 'person' masks across frames 1, 4, and 5, and in frame 2 the mask bleeds into the shadow/ground between the wearer's legs.
descriptions.pose: The pose map tracks the 2D skeletal keypoints of the camera wearer's hands (magenta) at roughly 0.4–0.8 m from the camera and attempts to place a body torso/head skeleton (yellow), operating in the same downward-looking outdoor scene where the wearer holds a dog toy above a dog positioned 0.6–1.5 m in front of them. In frames 1 and 2, two magenta hand skeletons capture the wearer's extended left hand holding the toy on the left and the lower right hand on the right; in frame 3 and frame 5, only one hand is detected (the lower right hand in frame 3 and the raised right hand holding the toy in frame 5), while in frame 4 both raised hands are detected near the center at about 0.4–0.5 m distance. When detected, the finger keypoints indicate the inward/upward orientation of the wearer's palms and fingers grasping the toy within arm's reach, which is harder to parse precisely in the motion-blurred RGB frames (such as the top-left hand in frame 1). However, the pose map is severely unreliable for overall scene understanding: it completely misses the wearer's left hand in frames 3 and 5, provides no skeletal keypoints for the wearer's actual torso or legs in frames 1–3 and 5, and offers no representation of the dog or the toy. Worse, in frame 4, the estimator hallucinates a yellow human torso and facial keypoint cluster directly over the leaping dog's head and the wearer's legs, falsely interpreting the dog looking toward the camera wearer as a facing human head and upper body.
